# What `provenance$coverage` holds

`cog_geographic_rollup()` and `cog_peer_compare()` attach a coverage table to their
provenance at `provenance$coverage`. It has one row per requested year and five
columns: `year`, `n_units_collected`, `n_units_reporting`, `n_units_expected` and
`is_census_year`. A second field, `provenance$coverage_mode`, records the `coverage`
argument you passed.

The table is built from the years you requested. A year in which none of your
governments has a row still gets a row in the table, with `n_units_reporting` equal
to zero.

Point `USCOGDATA_URL` at the bundled fixture corpus to run the examples without
network access or credentials. The fixture copies four full years of the published
corpus, FY2011, FY2012, FY2019 and FY2020, from its 2026-08-03 build. Its FY2012 and
FY2019 counts for Georgia cities and Police match the published corpus as of the
2026-10-26 build, except that the newer crosswalk lists 567 Georgia cities where the
fixture lists 566.

```{r}
library(uscogdata)

# Point at the bundled offline fixture. In real use, USCOGDATA_URL is set to the
# published corpus URL instead -- see README.md.
Sys.setenv(USCOGDATA_URL = paste0(
  system.file("extdata/fixture_corpus", package = "uscogdata"), "/"
))
```

# What each counter counts

Each counter answers a different question about the governments you named.

`n_units_expected` counts the governments you asked about. For
`cog_geographic_rollup()` it is the number of distinct ids across every layer of
`govids`. For `cog_peer_compare()` it is the number of peers. The target is the
subject of the comparison and is not counted.

`n_units_collected` counts how many of those governments have at least one spending
row in the corpus that year, in any category. The verb looks this up in the long view
behind `cog_spending()`, which holds every non-aggregate, non-intergovernmental
expenditure row. A government that Census did not collect from that year has no rows
there, whatever category you asked about.

`n_units_reporting` counts how many of those governments have at least one row in
the result for that year. The result holds only the category you requested, so this
counter depends on the category.

A government with a row in the result also has a row in the long view, so in every
year `n_units_reporting <= n_units_collected <= n_units_expected`.

# Three groups of governments

The counters split the governments you named into three groups each year:

1. `n_units_expected - n_units_collected` governments have no spending rows in the
   corpus that year. The Census of Governments collects from every government only
   in years ending in 2 or 7 and from a sample in other years, so in a sample year
   this group includes every government outside that year's sample.
2. `n_units_collected - n_units_reporting` governments were collected that year but
   have no rows in your category. A city that contracts its policing to the county
   sheriff lands here for `category = "Police"`. Its Police spending is a real zero.
3. `n_units_reporting` governments have rows in your category.

A government in the first group and a government in the second group look the same in
the result: neither has a row. Only `n_units_collected` tells them apart.

# Georgia cities and Police spending

Build the list of Georgia cities with `cog_gov_search()` and roll their Police
spending up for all four fixture years:

```{r}
ga_cities <- cog_gov_search(state = "GA", type = "city")
nrow(ga_cities)

police <- cog_geographic_rollup(
  govids   = list(city = ga_cities$canonical_govid),
  category = "Police",
  years    = c(2011, 2012, 2019, 2020)
)

coverage <- attr(police, "provenance")$coverage
coverage
```

On the fixture, `n_units_expected` is 566 in every year, because it counts the ids
you passed. FY2012 is a census year. Census collected 534 of the 566 cities, and 398
of those have Police rows. That leaves 32 cities in the first group and 136 in the
second. In the three sample years, Census collected 60 or 103 cities, and nearly all
of them have Police rows.

You can rebuild `n_units_collected` from the public verbs. The `"direct"` concept
covers every non-intergovernmental expenditure subtype, so asking `cog_spending()`
for every Direct category returns a row for each collected government:

```{r, message = FALSE}
direct <- cog_spending(
  ga_cities$canonical_govid,
  years = c(2011, 2012, 2019, 2020),
  category = "All Categories",
  expenditure_concept = "direct"
)
collected <- unique(direct[, c("year", "canonical_govid")])
table(collected$year)
```

The counts match the `n_units_collected` column above.

# Two ratios

Divide the counters to get two rates:

```{r}
coverage$collection_rate <- coverage$n_units_collected / coverage$n_units_expected
coverage$participation   <- coverage$n_units_reporting / coverage$n_units_collected
coverage[, c("year", "is_census_year", "collection_rate", "participation")]
```

The collection rate, `n_units_collected / n_units_expected`, is the share of the
governments you named that Census collected that year. It depends on the survey
calendar and the sample, and it is the same for every category. On the fixture it is
0.94 in FY2012 and between 0.11 and 0.18 in the sample years.

Category participation, `n_units_reporting / n_units_collected`, is the share of the
collected governments that have rows in your category. On the fixture, 0.75 of the
cities collected in FY2012 have Police rows.

Do not read `n_units_reporting / n_units_expected` as a response rate. It equals the
collection rate times category participation, so a low value can come from a sample
year, from a category many governments do not fund, or from both. For FY2012 it is
398 / 566, about 0.70, and the counters show that most of the shortfall is the 136
collected cities with no Police rows.

# Comparing a census year with a sample year

Participation is higher in the fixture's sample years than in FY2012: 1.00 in FY2011
and 0.93 in FY2019 and FY2020. The cities Census collects in a sample year are a
different set from the full universe. Join the collected cities to the population
estimate that `cog_gov_search()` returns:

```{r}
collected <- merge(collected, ga_cities[, c("canonical_govid", "population_acs")])
tapply(collected$population_acs, collected$year, median, na.rm = TRUE)
```

On the fixture, the median collected city has about 1,500 residents in FY2012 and
about 17,500 in FY2019 and FY2020. The sample years collect much larger cities than
the typical Georgia city, and a larger share of them report Police spending. A
sample-year participation rate describes the cities Census sampled that year, so use
a census year to estimate the share of all Georgia cities with Police spending.

To compare a census year with a sample year, hold the governments fixed. Take the
cities collected in both years and measure participation among them:

```{r}
both <- intersect(
  collected$canonical_govid[collected$year == 2012],
  collected$canonical_govid[collected$year == 2019]
)
length(both)

reported <- unique(police[, c("year", "canonical_govid")])
sapply(c(FY2012 = 2012, FY2019 = 2019), function(y) {
  mean(both %in% reported$canonical_govid[reported$year == y])
})
```

On the fixture, 99 Georgia cities were collected in both FY2012 and FY2019. Among
them, participation is 0.97 in FY2012 and 0.94 in FY2019, against 0.75 and 0.93 among
all collected cities. Once the cities are the same, the FY2019 rate is no longer
higher than the FY2012 rate.

The published corpus shows the same pattern for every US city. As of its 2026-10-26
build, Police participation among collected cities is 0.70, 0.73 and 0.72 in the
census years FY2012, FY2017 and FY2022, and between 0.93 and 0.95 in every sample year
from FY2013 to FY2023. Among the 3,867 cities collected in both FY2022 and FY2021, it
is 0.929 in FY2022 and 0.935 in FY2021. Fire, Libraries and Housing & Community behave
the same way: participation among the same cities moves by 0.01 or less between those
two years, while participation among all collected cities rises by 0.16 to 0.24.

Compare participation between two census years, or between the same governments in
two years. All collected governments in a census year and all collected governments
in a sample year are two different sets of cities.

# The FY2022 example on the published corpus

The reference pages for `cog_geographic_rollup()` and `cog_peer_compare()` describe
the same query for FY2022, a census year. The fixture does not carry FY2022, so the
query needs the published corpus:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Not run: needs USCOGDATA_URL set to the published corpus. The fixture has no FY2022.
ga_cities <- cog_gov_search(state = "GA", type = "city")
police_2022 <- cog_geographic_rollup(
  govids   = list(city = ga_cities$canonical_govid),
  category = "Police",
  years    = 2022
)
attr(police_2022, "provenance")$coverage
```

On the published corpus, as of its 2026-10-26 build, the chunk returns 567 expected,
535 collected and 393 reporting. The 174 cities without Police rows split into 32
that Census did not collect and 142 that were collected and have no Police rows. The
reference pages attribute most of the gap to cities that contract policing to the
county sheriff, and the counters place 142 of the 174 in the second group.

# Peer comparisons count peers only

In `cog_peer_compare()`, `n_units_expected` is the number of peers, and
`n_units_reporting` counts peer rows only. The target is left out of all three
counters. Compare Fitzgerald, Georgia, with the 12 Georgia cities closest to it in
FY2012 population:

```{r}
fitzgerald <- "132017204209"
peers <- cog_find_peers(fitzgerald, year = 2012, same_state = TRUE, max_peers = 12)
nrow(peers)

cmp <- cog_peer_compare(fitzgerald, peers, category = "Police", years = c(2012, 2019))
attr(cmp, "provenance")$coverage
```

All 12 peers were collected and report Police spending in FY2012. In FY2019, Census
collected four of them and three have Police rows. Eight peers fall in the first group
and one in the second. The `summary_p25`, `summary_p50` and `summary_p75` rows for
FY2019 are computed from those three peers' rows.

# What else changes the counters

`coverage = "census"` drops the sample years before the query runs, so the table has
one row per requested census year:

```{r}
census_only <- cog_geographic_rollup(
  govids   = list(city = ga_cities$canonical_govid),
  category = "Police",
  years    = c(2011, 2012, 2019, 2020),
  coverage = "census"
)
attr(census_only, "provenance")$coverage
```

`coverage = "consistent"` keeps only the governments with rows in every requested
year. The filter runs before the counters are computed, so `n_units_reporting` is the
same in every year. `n_units_expected` and `n_units_collected` are not filtered:

```{r}
balanced <- cog_geographic_rollup(
  govids   = list(city = ga_cities$canonical_govid),
  category = "Police",
  years    = c(2012, 2019),
  coverage = "consistent"
)
attr(balanced, "provenance")$coverage
```

On the fixture, 93 Georgia cities have Police rows in both FY2012 and FY2019. Under
`"consistent"`, `n_units_reporting / n_units_collected` no longer measures category
participation, because the numerator is filtered and the denominator is not.

`cog_peer_compare()` exempts the target from the `"consistent"` filter, and its
`summary_*` quantiles are computed after the filter.

With `per_capita = TRUE`, `cog_geographic_rollup()` drops rows whose government has
no population for that year before it counts `n_units_reporting`. Such a government
still counts as expected and collected. `cog_peer_compare()` does not drop these
rows.

# `is_census_year`

`is_census_year` is `TRUE` for years ending in 2 or 7. It describes the survey
calendar. Read `n_units_collected` to see how complete a year is: in FY2012, a census
year, the fixture has spending rows for 534 of its 566 Georgia cities.

# Summary

- `n_units_expected` is the number of governments you named, or the number of peers
  in `cog_peer_compare()`.
- `n_units_collected` is how many of them have any spending row that year.
- `n_units_reporting` is how many of them have a row in your category that year.
- `n_units_collected / n_units_expected` is the collection rate.
  `n_units_reporting / n_units_collected` is category participation among collected
  governments.
- `n_units_reporting / n_units_expected` mixes the two, so read the counters
  separately before you explain a gap.
- A sample year collects a different set of governments from a census year.
  Compare participation between census years, or between the same governments
  across years.
